He pointed out that the engineering industry has a "rainwater period" for typhoons and heavy rain that allows construction schedules to be postponed, and extreme heat should also be taken into consideration. He proposed that the government could take the lead in following up. He also suggested that the government should adjust the standards for the Work Heat Stress Warning according to outdoor workers, and advocated that employers who violate the rules should be subject to prosecution.

The hot weather has once again drawn attention to the working conditions of outdoor workers, with "Occupational Safety Heroes" bearing the brunt. Ho Ping-tak, who has been in the industry for many years, has expressed various opinions on the scaffolding trade. The government has recently intended to introduce metal scaffolding. On a very hot day, the most intuitive difference between metal scaffolding and bamboo scaffolding is the temperature, but what exactly is the difference?

"Metal scaffolding at construction sites can easily reach temperatures of 60-something to 70 degrees"

Ho Ping-tak said that in general, metal scaffolding at construction sites uses iron tube frames. Compared with the suspended aluminium frames used in small-scale repair works, the materials used are heavier and more heat-conductive. An iron tube waiting to be installed, when placed in direct sunlight without any nearby shade, "can easily reach temperatures of 60-something to 70 degrees."

Witnessed five out of seven workers suffer from heatstroke

Ho Ping-tak once visited a metal scaffolding construction site, where he stood on the rooftop and measured with a thermometer — 54.6 degrees. He also visited a site at Anderson Road, where seven people were working on the floor and five showed symptoms of heatstroke. He added that metal scaffolding absorbs far more heat than traditional bamboo scaffolding, and the level of difficulty in hot weather increases accordingly.

Construction sites offer ice cream and fruit to cool down — Ho Ping-tak: Only available at large sites. Ho Ping-tak pointed out that although some construction sites now install thermometers or wind speed displays around the area, and some companies even offer ice cream, fruit, and herbal tea to cool down, making working conditions seem to be gradually improving, these benefits are only available at large sites. Very few companies proactively require their employees to rest after the Labour Department issues a "Work Heat Stress Warning." In reality, workers still have to "come up with their own solutions," such as bringing their own neck fans, fan vests, and making ice bricks from large water bottles to bring to work.

He mentioned that the Labour Department established the "Work Heat Stress Warning" in 2023, and frontline workers were very happy at the time, saying, "Finally, the Labour Department is willing to speak up and fight for this heat stress warning for us frontline workers." He said workers had originally hoped that the warning would be like typhoon or rainstorm warnings, allowing construction sites to temporarily shut down. "But it turned out that more than 200 warnings have been issued, yet not a single one reached the red level, nor was anyone called to stop work." What's worse, even during the recent "highest temperature on record," there was only an amber warning.

Ho Ping-tak pointed out that temperatures vary in Central, at construction sites, and on the hill. Although he is not an expert, he questioned whether the mechanism for issuing the Work Heat Stress Warning should be adjusted according to the conditions of outdoor workers. "Some construction sites reach temperatures in the 50s. So when those so-called experts formulate measures, should they experience it themselves? It shouldn't be about sitting in an air-conditioned room evaluating some data. I think for any theory, to prove whether it's effective, practice is what matters most."

Rainwater period allows construction delays — Ho Ping-tak advocates government taking the lead to treat heat stress equally

Ho Ping-tak further pointed out that many companies in the industry have a concept of "rainwater period," meaning that after work stoppages due to typhoons or heavy rain, companies are allowed to postpone delivery deadlines. He explained that this practice exists because in the past, Hong Kong might have had five or six typhoons a year, and in severe weather, "bamboo can slip, and clamps can come loose." However, regarding hot weather, workers also become dizzy, yet there is no similar consideration. If a project is on a tight schedule, "it's too hot and you want to rest, but the construction period remains unchanged, the concrete pouring schedule remains unchanged, which makes many brothers and workers feel quite helpless."

He believes that the current heat stress warning is stuck in a situation of "following it is out of人情 (humanity), not following it is the rule," because construction delays are fined on a daily basis. Employers who do the maths and find that "even with full earnings they won't have enough to pay the fine (from the developer)" naturally choose to exploit workers. This also puts workers in a passive position. He suggested that the government consider making rest periods under the warning mandatory, and imposing fines on contractors who fail to comply. The government should also take the lead by allowing projects to be postponed without penalty during extreme heat conditions, so that contractors will follow suit.

Law Chin-sheng, Legislative Council member from the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, also agreed that even if the threshold for issuing the heat stress warning is revised, "I don't think it would be red every day? Maybe it's only 8 to 10 days at the hottest," and he believes the impact on the overall construction industry would be limited.
